title: I built animation software that lets you iteratively create and edit animations with AI
author: Crockiestar
selftext:
I've been working on a tool called **Warp Studio**, originally built to help with my own game development projects. The idea is pretty simple: **AI is incredibly powerful for creating things, but it's much more useful when you can actually control and iteratively edit what it creates.**

At the heart of Warp Studio is a smart mesh deformation system that makes animating both 2D artwork and 3D models incredibly easy. Instead of manually rigging, weight painting, or redrawing frames, you can place pins on a character and simply move them around. The surrounding mesh deforms naturally, making it possible to create complex movement with surprisingly little effort.

You can animate things yourself or have AI do the work through natural language prompts.

**One of the biggest discoveries I've made while developing this is just how much better AI performs when you give it powerful tools to work with.**

Instead of asking Codex or Claude Code to build an entire animation pipeline, write scaffolding, debug rendering systems, and run tests just to produce an animation, you can give it access to software that already handles all of that and makes it easier for it to work with.

It's a similar reason why AI can accomplish so much when connected to Blender through MCP. The AI can focus on actually creating rather than constantly reinventing the tooling.

Warp Studio has full MCP support, meaning you can connect tools like ChatGPT Codex or Claude Code and have them directly operate the software.

There are a few different workflows built into the app:

* **Warp Puppet:** Take a 2D character, automatically separate it into parts, rig it, and animate it using AI or manual controls.
* **Warp Animate:** Import a single image and quickly animate it with smart mesh deformation, pin movements, and automatic tweening.
* **Warp Director:** Build and animate complete editable scenes, including multiple characters, backgrounds, and effects.
* **Warp 3D:** Import 3D models and animate them using smart mesh deformation without traditional rigging or weight painting.

You can combine these workflows, make manual adjustments, ask AI to change specific things, and keep refining the result without starting over.

The goal is to bring the level of creative control you'd expect from software like Adobe Animate or Spine into an AI-native workflow, rather than treating AI generation as a one-shot process.

Everything is designed around producing editable work that can ultimately be exported into game-ready animations and assets.

I think the future of AI-assisted game development isn't just prompting AI to make finished assets. It's having powerful creative software that AI can actually use alongside you.

Warp Studio: [https://crockiestar.itch.io/warp-studio](https://crockiestar.itch.io/warp-studio)

replies.author: Crockiestar
replies.body: Yea so Warp 3D uses smart voxel based ARAP mesh deformation instead of traditional bones, rigging, or weight painting. You can import an unrigged 3D model, place a few pins, and immediately start moving limbs around while the mesh naturally bends and preserves its shape. It's much easier for both you and the AI to produce good-looking animations quickly, and you can iteratively refine everything through MCP. I genuinely think more 3D software will adopt techniques like this. And yeah, nothing's stopping you from building something similar in Blender! You could ask Claude to experiment with voxel-based ARAP deformation using pins, though getting it working well is the tricky part. Warp Studio just brings this together with 2D animation, auto-rigging, scene creation, and AI-driven workflows in one app.

comments.author: Reasonable_Damage_18
comments.body:
I've actually wanted to build a tool like this for quite a while. After looking through your feature overview, I think it looks really promising!

I do have a few thoughts and suggestions that I hope you'll find helpful.

1. **Lowering the skill barrier:** My main goal is to use AI and animation tools to create fun, high-quality animations that match what I have in mind, without having to rely on my own animation skills.
2. **AI-powered animation generation:** Ideally, I should be able to describe an action in plain language, and the AI, working together with the animation tools, would automatically generate smooth, natural-looking skeletal animations or frame-by-frame animations.
3. **Automated asset preparation and rigging:** For example, if I provide a single flat character image, the tool should be able to automatically separate it into individual body parts, generate any missing or hidden parts, place the appropriate bones and joints, and create a usable rig that I can animate and control.

If a tool could handle these three things well, I believe there would be significant demand for it, especially among indie game developers and creators who don't have professional animation skills.

Otherwise, existing solutions like GPT-generated animation frames are already pretty decent, so the real value would be in making the entire animation workflow easier, more automated, and more controllable.

comments.author: TPM2209
comments.body: Does this program use diffusion models in any way? It doesn't look like it does, but I wanted to ask. I have a bit of a hard line against using diffusion models in my own projects specifically.

replies.author: Crockiestar
replies.body: Nope! The AI-assisted rigging, animation, and mesh deformation don't use diffusion models. They're based on manipulating geometry and moving pins around. I have added optional AI image generation/editing through Gemini or ChatGPT in the image editor, but you never have to use those features. Warp Director can also create some pretty complex animated SVG scenes using math and procedural animation rather than diffusion. So you can absolutely use Warp Studio without relying on diffusion models.

comments.author: SoloDev_Sg
comments.body:
As someone with absolutely no art background, I have a few questions:

1. Accessibility for non-artists: How user-friendly is this tool for a complete beginner who can't draw and knows nothing about traditional rigging or animation principles? Can I just import a generated image or model and let the AI handle everything else (separating parts, placing pins, and designing the actual movements)?
2. Underlying logic of the 3D assets: In the Warp 3D workflow, what is the fundamental difference between your output 3D assets and the standard pipeline assets used in game engines (Skeletal Mesh + Skeleton + Physics Asset)? Does Warp generate traditional bone weights, or does it rely on something like Vertex Animation or a custom mesh deformation format?
3. Unreal Engine workflow: If I bring Warp-animated 3D assets into Unreal Engine, can I still use the classic workflow on the logic side (Skeletal Mesh + Animation Blueprint + State Machines)? Or would these animations need a dedicated Warp plugin or custom rendering pipeline to run in-engine?

replies.author: Crockiestar
replies.body: Great questions! I actually built Warp Studio for my own game development projects because I think moving characters with smart mesh deformation and automatic tweening is one of the easiest and fastest ways to animate. Just place a couple of pins on a character and start dragging them around and you'll see what I mean! For beginners, you can import an image and have AI help separate it into parts, rig it, place pins, and create animations, or do it all manually without needing to understand traditional rigging. For 3D, Warp uses smart mesh deformation instead of traditional bones and weight painting, allowing you to animate models directly. It exports animated GLB/GLTF files, which Unreal Engine supports, although using them with traditional Animation Blueprints and State Machines may require additional setup. The whole idea is to make animation as simple and accessible as possible, whether you're animating manually or working alongside AI.

replies.author: SeasonedAdManager
replies.body:
Here is what my initiation and coordinator process works. I use a command called /game-init to start any new game and get things set up, with lots of sub-skills.

**TL;DR:** `/game-init` is a Claude Code skill I wrote. It asks me only about the game, makes every technical choice itself, writes a set of files that act as the project's memory, then goes straight on to building something playable. Running a "coordinator" chat with worker chats is an optional layer on top. By default one chat just works the task cards in order.

---

## What /game-init actually does

1. **Looks around without reporting.** It checks the engine and version, the git state, existing docs, and whether the `backlog` CLI is installed.
2. **Asks up to 4 rounds of game questions** (max 4 per round, each with a recommended answer first):
    * **The game:** core fantasy ("you are a ... who ..."), the main verb, platform and controls
    * **The feel:** 2 or 3 reference games, how you win and lose
    * **First playable:** the 30-second loop
    * **The look:** 2D or 3D, mood words

    If I say "I don't know", it picks a default and logs it as OPEN in a decisions file. It never asks about tests, hooks, folder layout or tooling. Those are its call.
3. **Builds the scaffold with no confirm step.** It never overwrites a file; if one already exists, it writes `<name>.proposed.md` next to it.
4. **Writes 4 starter cards:** Setup, First playable, Second playable step, Look. Art direction waits until I've played something.
5. **Runs the check script, then starts building cards 1 and 2 in the same chat.** It ends with a short plain-English note: what I can play, which keys to press, what to look for.

### Files it creates

| File | Job |
|---|---|
| `AGENTS.md` (+ `CLAUDE.md` = `@AGENTS.md`) | Rules every chat reads, under 80 lines |
| `STATE.md` | Snapshot of 15 lines or fewer: active card, blocker, next action |
| `backlog/tasks/` | Cards, each sized to fit one chat session |
| `tools/check.sh` | One pass/fail check for build and tests |
| `.claude/settings.json` hooks | Block hand edits to scene files, stop a chat from ending without a check, warn at 40% and 50% context |
| `.claude/agents/` | verifier (Haiku), reviewer (Sonnet, read-only), asset-lint (Haiku) |
| `.obsidian/` + vault MCP | Project root doubles as an Obsidian vault (more below) |

The main idea is that **the files are the memory.** No chat holds state. Any fresh chat picks up from `AGENTS.md` + `STATE.md` + the current card. That's what makes it cheap to throw a chat away when its context gets full.

### Obsidian vault

The project root is also an Obsidian vault, so `STATE.md`, the cards, the decisions log and the design docs all read as linked notes. `/game-init` sets it up automatically:

* Writes `.obsidian/app.json` with ignore filters for art, evidence, engine caches and `.claude/`, so the vault only shows notes
* Adds `.obsidian/` to `.git/info/exclude` so it stays out of the repo
* Registers the vault with Obsidian so it shows up in the vault list
* Adds an MCP connector for every chat: `claude mcp add --scope user <game>-vault -- npx -y @bitbonsai/mcpvault@0.16.0 <project root>`

Two things this gets you: I can follow the whole project in Obsidian without opening the code, and chats use the connector's search and outline tools to find past decisions instead of reading whole files, which saves tokens. Docs and the decisions log link to each other with `[[wikilinks]]`; cards keep plain file names so the backlog format doesn't break.

### The rest of the skill chain

* `/game-work`: plans the card into the card file, builds, runs the check, updates the card and state, moves on to the next card. It only stops for game design questions, spending money, or "play this and tell me how it feels".
* `/game-verify`: three tiers, cheapest first: the check script, a scripted scenario, a screenshot or clip
* `/game-handoff`: writes the card log and `STATE.md`, then prints a one-line resume prompt for a fresh chat
* `/game-plan`: turns a new feature into a few cards, each sized to one session

---

## Running a coordinator

The lead chat gets titled `<GAME> · COORDINATOR` and pinned in the sidebar. With worker chats:

1. **The coordinator owns `STATE.md`, the board and merging.** It does not build anything itself.
2. **One worker chat per card.** In the Claude Code desktop app I use "chips", background tasks you click to spin off into their own session. Each prompt is basically: `Read AGENTS.md and STATE.md. Run /game-work on task-N.`
3. **The coordinator subscribes to each worker** so it gets notified when the worker goes idle.
4. **Every worker ends by messaging the coordinator** with: card id, branch, check output, evidence, decisions made. It does this even when blocked. Workers never start other chats.
5. **On each report the coordinator merges**, reruns the check, updates state and starts the next card.

When the coordinator reaches 50% context, it hands off: it lists the running workers in `STATE.md`, starts a fresh coordinator, and keeps its title until the new one confirms it has taken over.

---

## What makes it efficient

* **Only run cards in parallel when their files don't overlap.** Each card lists the files it owns. Two cards touching the same scene run one after the other.
* **Keep the coordinator thin.** It reads reports, merges, and hands checks to a cheap Haiku subagent, so its context lasts many cards.
* **One card = one context window**, roughly 10 files or fewer. If a worker hits 50% context, the card was too big. Split it.
* **Verify with the cheapest check that answers the question.** The check script runs on every change. Screenshots are only for "does it look right", because images cost a lot of tokens.
* **2 or 3 workers is the practical cap.** Merges happen one at a time and each worker needs a click to start, so more workers mostly means more waiting.

## Known rough edges

* Nothing in the templates explicitly gives the coordinator permission to merge, so add a line to `AGENTS.md` that does.
* There's no branch or worktree rule yet. Give each worker its own git worktree on a `card/<id>` branch, or parallel workers will overwrite each other's work in a shared checkout.

No, you only pay once to buy the software, and then everything is free to use forever. No credits, no subscriptions, no export fees, and no hidden costs. You can animate, render, and export as much as you want, completely locally and offline.

The credits you briefly saw in the video were from an old version of the software that I used to host online. That system no longer exists. The only exception is if you *choose* to connect an external AI service like ChatGPT or Gemini, which may have its own costs or usage limits. That's entirely optional and not required to use any of the core tools.

Buy it once, own it, and use it as much as you want.

comments.body:
Purchased it yesterday and can confirm it runs fine (at least based on my very limited testing) on Linux using Wine (GE-Proton11-3).

u/Crockiestar, are there any video guides on how to use it? I found just two on YouTube, but they're about a year old.

Some suggestions:

1. Local AI for image generation - something like Qwen Image Edit should work in theory, but we'd need to figure out the API, as there seem to be a whole bunch of different options. Maybe using the default ComfyUI Qwen Image Edit workflow would make things simpler.

2. Local AI text model support - ideally connected the same way as Gemini/Codex, with another place to enter OpenAI-compatible API credentials.

3. Headless mode — maybe add a parameter to the .exe that enables access through a browser without any shenanigans. For now, I had to spoof `X-Warp-Desktop-Token` and manually add it to the browser headers. (I only did this because I'm not a fan of how the Wine window looked, and it was also getting annoying with the Codex auth popups :) )

4. Maybe consider open-sourcing it?

5. I played around with Warp 3D, and the main problem I ran into is that the generated animation files are very large. For example, the unrigged file is \~120 KB, while the resulting 47-frame walking animation is 7.5 MB. That seems like quite a lot.

I'll check out the 2D stuff later if I have some free time.

replies.author: Crockiestar
replies.body:
Thanks so much for purchasing and for all the great feedback! Really cool to hear it's working on Linux through Wine too!

I originally built Warp Studio as a tool to help with my own game development projects, so tutorials and documentation haven't been a huge focus yet. I definitely plan on making more videos showing how to use the different features!

Local AI support is something I'd love to expand, especially through ComfyUI and OpenAI-compatible APIs. Warp already supports MCP for connecting local AI agents, but making that process easier would be great. Headless mode is an interesting suggestion too!

As for Warp 3D, I'll definitely look into optimizing the animation export sizes.

Really appreciate you taking the time to test everything and share your suggestions! Feedback like this is super helpful!
